strengths: The paper targets an important and practical inefficiency in text-to-image diffusion: prompt adherence is usually assessed only after full generation. Early language-to-latent scoring could be useful for Best-of-N selection and adaptive generation pipelines.

The proposed NoisyCLIP approach is simple and plausible: fine-tuning the visual tower of a CLIP/SigLIP-style dual encoder on intermediate SDXL latents converted to RGB-like representations. This makes the method easy to understand and potentially easy to reproduce if the promised data/code are released.

The manuscript contributes not only a method but also noisy-latent benchmark datasets derived from Conceptual Captions and GenAI-Bench, including intermediate latent trajectories. This is a useful direction because standardized intermediate-generation data are currently scarce.

The experiments address several relevant settings: language-to-latent ranking over denoising steps, Best-of-N selection under reduced denoising cost, factual consistency with corrupted captions, latent-range ablations, backbone comparison, encoder-training ablations, and qualitative failure cases.

The main empirical result is promising: selecting around the middle of denoising reportedly preserves most of the final-image CLIP/VQAScore selection quality while reducing diffusion iterations substantially, and NoisyCLIP clearly outperforms frozen CLIP on noisy latents.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. The core method is essentially contrastive fine-tuning of an existing dual encoder on linearly decoded noisy latents. This is useful, but the paper sometimes frames it more strongly than the methodological contribution supports.

The evaluation relies heavily on automated proxy metrics, especially VQAScore and CLIP-style scores, rather than human preference or human prompt-adherence judgments. Since the method itself is a learned alignment metric, stronger validation against human judgments would be important.

The claimed computational savings are somewhat idealized. Cost is measured mainly as denoising iterations, but the overhead of latent conversion, encoder scoring, batch scheduling, and practical pipeline integration is not quantified. Wall-clock latency, memory, and throughput measurements would make the efficiency claim more convincing.

Generalization is insufficiently established. Most results appear tied to SDXL, one generation setup, and particular denoising ranges. It is unclear how robust NoisyCLIP is across different diffusion backbones, schedulers, resolutions, guidance scales, prompt distributions, or latent parameterizations.

The baselines are limited. The paper compares mainly against frozen CLIP/SigLIP on latent or final images, but does not thoroughly compare with recent latent feedback/alignment methods, VLM-based verifiers under comparable compute, learned reward models, or simpler alternatives such as training only on decoded intermediate images without the proposed framing.

The factual consistency result, while improved over CLIP, remains modest in absolute terms: R@1 around 0.506 midway through generation. This tempers claims that the method robustly understands fine-grained factual consistency, especially for counts, negation, and multi-entity prompts.

The benchmark and training data construction need more detail for reproducibility: exact latent storage format, scheduler settings, seed handling, prompt rewriting quality control, train/test overlap checks, and whether generated images or latents introduce artifacts that favor the proposed method.

The paper contains clarity and polish issues, including grammatical errors, typos in figures/tables, and occasional overclaiming. Some figures are difficult to interpret from the text alone, and several percentage improvements are reported without enough statistical uncertainty or significance analysis.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant efficiency problem in text-to-image diffusion: detecting poor prompt adherence before completing all denoising steps, especially for Best-of-N sampling where wasted compute can be substantial.

The core empirical idea is simple and potentially useful: fine-tune the visual tower of a CLIP-like model on intermediate noisy/denoised latent representations, while keeping the text tower fixed, then use it to rank partial generations.

The authors attempt to construct and release benchmark data with intermediate latent trajectories for Conceptual Captions and GenAI-Bench prompts, which could be useful if documented and released cleanly.

The paper includes several ablations over latent training ranges, backbone choice, encoder freezing, and qualitative failure cases; the limitations around CLIP-style weaknesses such as counting and negation are at least partially acknowledged.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method is essentially contrastive fine-tuning of CLIP’s image encoder on RGB-projected noisy latents. The paper frames this as a new framework, but does not convincingly distinguish it from straightforward latent/noisy-image CLIP adaptation or from closely related latent CLIP and online feedback work.

The evidence for the headline efficiency claim is weak. Computational cost is measured only as denoising step count, ignoring the cost of latent decoding/projection, NoisyCLIP scoring, batching, memory overhead, and realistic scheduling. The claimed “50% cost reduction” is therefore not a demonstrated wall-clock or throughput result.

The Best-of-N setting is oversimplified. The method appears to select a candidate at a fixed intermediate step and continue only that one; this is not the same as robust early stopping, dynamic pruning, or adaptive generation control. The paper’s language overclaims “real-time alignment assessment” and “early termination” relative to the actual experiments.

The evaluation depends heavily on automatic proxy metrics, mainly VQAScore and CLIP-like scores, with no human preference or prompt-adherence study. Since the method itself is CLIP-family contrastive scoring, the paper needs stronger independent validation to show that improvements are meaningful rather than metric-specific.

The baselines are inadequate. Comparing against frozen CLIP/SigLIP on noisy latent projections is a low bar. The paper lacks stronger alternatives such as decoding intermediate latents then applying final-image metrics, lightweight learned regressors, calibration baselines, existing latent CLIP/control methods, or VLM-based verification at reduced resolution/frequency.

Generalization is underexplored. Training and evaluation are tied to SDXL-generated latents and specific latent-to-RGB projection choices. There is no convincing evidence that NoisyCLIP transfers across diffusion architectures, schedulers, guidance scales, numbers of denoising steps, resolutions, or prompt distributions.

The benchmark contribution is not yet reproducible from the manuscript. Important details about dataset generation, seeds, filtering, prompt rewriting quality control, latent storage format, licensing, and splits are insufficient, and the paper only states that code/data “will be available.”

Several claims and numbers are confusing or inconsistent. The abstract claims 98% of CLIP alignment performance, while Table 1 suggests roughly 95% for one Best-of-N setting; other sections report percentage differences without clear denominators or uncertainty. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance over seeds.

The mathematical formulation is loose. The paper describes Phi as a linear transformation or inverse of the autoencoder mapping latents to RGB-like space, but this is not a true inverse of the encoder and its exact implementation matters substantially. The connection to cross-attention and “mimicking” diffusion conditioning is asserted rather than established.

The paper’s writing and presentation are below the expected standard for ECCV. There are numerous typos and awkward phrases, including “missalignments,” “assessement,” “genetation,” “aligment,” and repeated grammatical issues. These do not alone determine rejection, but they reinforce concerns about rigor and polish.

The practical impact is uncertain. Best-of-N itself multiplies generation cost, and the proposed method only partially recovers this cost while relying on additional training and scoring infrastructure. The paper does not show deployment-oriented measurements or compare against simply generating fewer candidates, using faster samplers, or applying cheaper final-image rerankers.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and practically relevant inefficiency in text-to-image diffusion: alignment failures are usually detected only after full denoising. Framing prompt-to-latent alignment as an in-process scoring problem is well motivated and useful for Best-of-N generation.

NoisyCLIP is technically simple but convincing: fine-tuning only the visual tower on noisy latent RGB projections preserves the text encoder and yields measurable improvements over frozen CLIP/SigLIP baselines in noisy latent stages. The method is easy to integrate into existing diffusion pipelines.

The experimental evidence supports the main efficiency claim reasonably well. In BoN settings, the method achieves close to final-image CLIP selection quality at substantially lower denoising cost, including the headline result of roughly 50% fewer diffusion iterations for about 98% of the final-image alignment score.

The proposed Noisy-Conceptual-Captions and Noisy-GenAI-Bench datasets are a meaningful contribution because intermediate latent trajectories are rarely available in standardized form. This could help future work compare early alignment metrics under controlled conditions.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond the main result: factual-consistency caption selection, latent-range ablations, encoder-freezing ablations, model-size analysis, backbone comparison with SigLIP, and split-level GenAI-Bench results. These make the empirical story more credible than a single BoN plot.
The writing is generally clear and the motivation is accessible. Figures and qualitative examples help explain why early latent scoring can be useful for selecting prompt-adherent generations.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies heavily on automatic alignment metrics, especially VQAScore and CLIP-like scoring, without human preference or human prompt-adherence validation. Since the proposed model is itself a contrastive text-vision scorer, stronger evidence is needed that improvements translate to actual perceptual alignment rather than metric-specific gains.

The cost analysis counts denoising steps but does not fully account for the overhead of running NoisyCLIP, latent-to-RGB projection, batching effects, memory/storage of latent trajectories, or wall-clock latency. The claimed computational savings are plausible, but the practical speedup is not directly measured.

The method is evaluated only with SDXL-style latent diffusion and a specific 50-step setup. It remains unclear how well the approach transfers to other diffusion backbones, schedulers, resolutions, guidance scales, or newer text-to-image models with different latent spaces and conditioning mechanisms.

The novelty claim is somewhat overstated. Prior work has explored latent-space guidance, latent scoring, and CLIP-based feedback during generation; the paper’s contribution is better described as a systematic benchmark and fine-tuned latent alignment scorer rather than a wholly new paradigm.

Some reported gains are modest in absolute terms, often around 1-3 VQAScore points, and the paper does not report confidence intervals, repeated training runs, or significance tests. This makes it hard to judge robustness, especially for the smaller improvements in BoN selection.

The factual-consistency results show improvement but also reveal substantial remaining limitations: R@1 around 0.5 in mid-generation is useful but far from reliable, and known CLIP weaknesses such as counting and negation persist. The paper could be more explicit about when early stopping would be unsafe.

The datasets are described as future/open resources, but reproducibility depends on their actual release, generation prompts, seeds, scheduler details, latent extraction format, and code. The paper would be stronger with more complete release details and a clearer reproducibility checklist.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and practically important problem: avoiding wasted computation in diffusion Best-of-N generation by estimating prompt-latent alignment before full denoising. This is a meaningful applied/systems contribution even though the core method is simple fine-tuning of a twin-tower encoder.

NoisyCLIP is technically plausible and well motivated. Training only the visual tower on noisy intermediate latents while keeping the text tower fixed is a sensible design choice, and the latent-range ablation supports the choice of training on steps 20-29.

The experiments cover several useful settings: language-to-latent ranking, factual caption retrieval, Best-of-N selection, backbone transfer to SigLIP, and zero-shot application to SD3.5/FLUX-style DiT models. The reported gains over CLIP and LatentCLIP in mid-generation selection are consistent across multiple tables.

The proposed Noisy-Conceptual-Captions and Noisy-GenAI-Bench resources, if released with latents and generation metadata, could be valuable for standardizing evaluation of in-process diffusion alignment metrics.
The paper includes helpful qualitative examples, failure cases, and a small human preference study, which makes the automatic-metric results easier to interpret.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The method is essentially contrastive fine-tuning of an existing CLIP/SigLIP visual encoder on linearly decoded noisy latents. The main contribution is the dataset/protocol plus application to early stopping, rather than a fundamentally new model or learning objective.

The experimental case relies heavily on VQAScore and CLIP-like/VLM-based automatic evaluation. Since the proposed model is itself a CLIP-style scorer and the task is selecting images according to another learned scorer, the evidence would be stronger with larger human evaluation, confidence intervals, and analysis of when VQAScore disagrees with humans.

The human study is too limited for the strength of the claims: only 100 image pairs from the GenAI-Bench Basic split are reported, with little detail about annotator count, tie rate, prompt coverage, or statistical significance.

The cost analysis is somewhat idealized. It counts denoising iterations but does not clearly include the overhead of latent RGB transformation, VAE decoding for DiT generalization, running NoisyCLIP over all candidates, batching effects, memory/storage of intermediate latents, or wall-clock measurements. This weakens the claim of 50% compute reduction in practical deployments.

The benchmark construction needs more rigor. The paper uses generated images and LLM-corrupted prompts, but does not fully establish label quality, filtering, licensing/release constraints, or whether the corruptions are always valid and uniquely distinguishable. The new datasets are also relatively small for a benchmark claim.

Several comparisons are missing or underdeveloped: cheap partial-decode plus frozen CLIP, lower-resolution/preview decoding, direct regression to final VQAScore, diffusion-internal confidence/attention metrics, and stronger VLM reward models used as early rankers. These would help show that NoisyCLIP is not only better than standard CLIP/LatentCLIP at unsuitable timesteps.

Some reported improvements are small in absolute terms, especially in the Best-of-N skill tables, and the paper does not report variance over seeds/prompts or statistical tests. This makes it hard to judge robustness of 1-2% gains.

Clarity is generally acceptable, but important implementation details are scattered or underspecified, including exact latent indexing conventions, RGB latent transform details, release format for the datasets, and precise Best-of-N stopping policy across N and timestep budgets.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant efficiency problem in text-to-image diffusion: post-hoc Best-of-N selection wastes computation on samples that could potentially be rejected earlier.
The core direction, fine-tuning a CLIP/SigLIP-style image encoder on noisy intermediate latents for prompt-latent scoring, is simple and potentially useful for practical inference-time selection.

The manuscript evaluates on several settings: factual caption selection, Best-of-N ranking, different latent ranges, CLIP/SigLIP backbones, and zero-shot transfer to SD3.5 and FLUX. The appendix includes useful per-skill breakdowns and failure cases.
The proposed noisy-latent datasets could be valuable if released with clear generation metadata and splits.
weaknesses: The contribution is technically modest: NoisyCLIP is essentially contrastive fine-tuning of an existing twin-tower encoder on linearly decoded noisy latents. The paper frames this as a new architecture and continuous monitoring tool, but the algorithmic novelty is limited and the mechanism is not deeply analyzed.

The main acceptance issue is the strength of evidence. Most headline gains are small, often around 1-3 VQAScore points, and no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or statistical tests are reported. The human study is only 100 pairs from the GenAI-Bench Basic split and lacks key details such as annotator count, tie rate, instructions, and sampling protocol.

Several claims are overstated or internally inconsistent. The abstract says half-cost NoisyCLIP matches or beats full-cost frozen CLIP, but the main text reports a roughly 2% drop versus 300-step CLIP/LatentCLIP in Figure 6, and the appendix tables show final-image CLIP/LatentCLIP outperforming mid-generation NoisyCLIP on many categories.

The evaluation relies heavily on VQAScore as the arbiter of alignment while training and baselines are CLIP-family models. This leaves open whether the method improves actual human-perceived prompt adherence rather than optimizing agreement with one automatic evaluator. The limited human evaluation does not sufficiently resolve this.

The Best-of-N early-stopping protocol is underspecified and somewhat idealized. The paper counts only diffusion denoising iterations, omitting the cost of latent decoding/transformation and scoring; it is unclear how thresholds or selection steps are chosen in a deployable early-stopping system rather than a fixed-rank selection experiment.

Baselines are not fully convincing. Comparing against frozen CLIP on noisy linear-RGB latents and LatentCLIP trained for clean final latents is expected to favor a model explicitly trained on noisy latents. Missing baselines include simple noise-augmented CLIP fine-tuning variants, calibration/regression to final CLIP/VQAScore, lightweight denoising before CLIP, and stronger preference/reward models used at intermediate decoded states.

The dataset and reproducibility details are insufficient for the scale of the claims. The paper mentions 50k uniformly sampled latents and generated benchmark latents, but does not clearly specify train/test separation, prompt filtering, exact latent indexing convention, seeds, generation settings, release status, or whether generated images used to create the benchmark overlap semantically with training captions.

The method has important limitations that are acknowledged only lightly: it inherits CLIP weaknesses on counting and negation, can select hallucinated or incomplete images, and may not generalize robustly across schedulers, resolutions, guidance scales, or diffusion models without VAE decoding. These limitations directly affect the claimed role as an early rejection criterion.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical bottleneck in diffusion-based text-to-image generation: prompt-alignment failures are usually detected only after expensive full denoising. The proposed early language-to-latent scoring problem is well motivated and clearly connected to test-time scaling/Best-of-N workflows.

NoisyCLIP is technically simple but effective: fine-tuning the visual tower on noisy decoded latents while freezing the text tower is a plausible design, and the paper provides useful analysis of which latent ranges are best for training and inference.

The experimental evidence is fairly broad for an algorithms/general contribution. The paper evaluates language-to-latent alignment, factual caption retrieval, Best-of-N early stopping, backbone transfer to SigLIP, and zero-shot use on SD3.5 and FLUX, with appendix breakdowns over GenAI-Bench skill categories.

The reported efficiency/quality tradeoff is compelling: at roughly half the denoising cost in Best-of-N settings, NoisyCLIP retains most of the final-image selection quality and outperforms CLIP/LatentCLIP at comparable intermediate budgets.

The two proposed noisy-latent benchmarks are a useful community-facing contribution if released as described, since intermediate diffusion trajectories are rarely standardized and are hard to compare reproducibly across papers.

The paper is generally clear, with intuitive figures and qualitative examples including failure cases. The appendix adds helpful details on prompt corruptions, skill-level performance, model-size ablations, and a small human preference study.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate. The method is essentially contrastive fine-tuning of a CLIP-like visual encoder on linearly/VAE-decoded noisy latents, and much of the contribution rests on dataset construction and system use rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

The strongest claims rely heavily on automatic metrics, especially VQAScore and CLIP-like similarity measures. These are reasonable, but they may share biases with the trained model family; the human evaluation is small, limited to 100 Basic-split pairs, and does not cover advanced prompts, factuality, or the full early-stopping setting.

The evaluation could better separate gains from the proposed method versus properties of the generated benchmark. Training uses SDXL-generated latents and substantial evaluation is also on SDXL-derived data; the SD3.5/FLUX transfer results are encouraging but summarized briefly and appear limited.

The paper does not make fully clear how training/test splits avoid overlap when both training and Noisy-Conceptual-Captions derive from Conceptual Captions-style data. This matters because the benchmark and training distribution are closely related.

The Best-of-N protocol is useful but simplified: cost is counted only as denoising steps, without wall-clock overhead from latent decoding/scoring, batching effects, memory cost, or realistic scheduler/pipeline integration. The claimed 50% compute reduction would be stronger with measured latency and throughput.

Some baselines are not perfectly matched. LatentCLIP is designed for clean or late latents, while NoisyCLIP is trained exactly for noisy intermediate latents; a stronger comparison would include similarly fine-tuned latent/noisy variants or alternative lightweight verifier baselines trained under the same data budget.

The method inherits known CLIP weaknesses, especially counting, negation, and attribute binding, as the authors note. These limitations are important because many alignment failures in text-to-image generation are compositional rather than object-recognition failures.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript as provided: dataset/model release locations, exact generation seeds/settings, prompt filtering, and full benchmark construction details would need to be explicit for the proposed benchmark to have lasting value.
